title: Sampling distribution of sample proportion for coupon redemption
scenario_markdown: A retail e-commerce marketing manager establishes that $p = 0.30$ ($30\%$) of all active customer accounts redeem digital promotional coupons. In an audit of customer discount engagement, an analyst surveys an independent random sample of $n = 200$ customer accounts.
assumptions: Independent random sample of customer accounts from a large account base
Success-failure conditions np >= 10 and n(1 - p) >= 10 are satisfied, justifying normal approximation for sample proportion p_hat
source_refs: Course Module 4: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

stages.prompt_markdown: Why is the normal approximation justified for modeling the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ in this study?

options.text_markdown: Both expected successes $np = 200(0.30) = 60$ and expected failures $n(1 - p) = 200(0.70) = 140$ are at least 10, satisfying the success-failure condition.
Any sample size with $n \ge 30$ guarantees normality for proportions, regardless of the value of $p$.
options.hint_markdown: For proportions, sample size alone ($n \ge 30$) is not sufficient if $p$ is extremely close to 0 or 1; you must check that both $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$.

options.text_markdown: The normal approximation requires the population proportion to be exactly $p = 0.50$.
options.hint_markdown: While $p = 0.50$ is most symmetric, any $p$ is valid for the normal approximation as long as $np$ and $n(1-p)$ both meet the threshold.

stages.explanation_markdown: The Central Limit Theorem applies to sample proportions when both the expected number of successes $np = 200 \times 0.30 = 60$ and failures $n(1 - p) = 200 \times 0.70 = 140$ are at least 10 (or $\ge 5$ under relaxed conventions). Here both 60 and 140 exceed the threshold, ensuring the binomial distribution is sufficiently symmetric for the normal approximation.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the standard error of the sample proportion $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ for this sample of $n = 200$ accounts?

options.hint_markdown: $\sqrt{np(1-p)} \approx 6.48$ is the standard deviation of the count of successes $X$, not the sample proportion $\hat{p} = X/n$.
$0.00105$ is the variance of the sample proportion $\sigma_{\hat{p}}^2$; remember to take the square root to obtain the standard error.

stages.explanation_markdown: The standard error of a sample proportion is $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.30 \times 0.70}{200}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.21}{200}} = \sqrt{0.00105} \approx 0.0324$ (or $3.24\%$). In Excel, this can be computed as `=SQRT(0.30 * 0.70 / 200)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the probability that more than $35\%$ of the sampled accounts redeem promotional coupons, $P(\hat{p} > 0.35)$?

options.hint_markdown: The question asks for the probability that the proportion exceeds $0.35$, which is the upper tail area $1 - \Phi(1.54)$, not the lower cumulative area.
Do not divide the one-tailed tail probability by 2; the question asks strictly for the single upper tail $P(\hat{p} > 0.35)$.

stages.explanation_markdown: Standardizing gives $Z = \frac{\hat{p} - p}{\sigma_{\hat{p}}} = \frac{0.35 - 0.30}{0.0324} = \frac{+0.05}{0.0324} \approx +1.54$. From the standard normal table, $\Phi(1.54) = 0.9382$. Therefore, the upper tail probability is $P(\hat{p} > 0.35) = 1 - \Phi(1.54) = 1 - 0.9382 = 0.0618$ (or $6.18\%$). Excel formula: `=1 - NORM.DIST(0.35, 0.30, SQRT(0.30 * 0.70 / 200), TRUE)` or `=1 - NORM.S.DIST(1.54, TRUE)`.
